title: Chunk Ladder
context: Grade 4, the hardest topic in the chapter. An adult sees a two-digit divisor, which looks like only a harder long division. What is actually new is that the times table for the divisor is not known by heart, so each step is found by trying multiples until one is too big, and a step that is not stated clearly loses the leftover that makes the next number. The worked example for this topic states its remainder at the first and last steps and skips it at the middle one, where nine tens are left and become the ninety-four ones divided next. The partial quotient method then lets a child use chunks they can work out, and the chunks always add up to the same quotient.

writeup.why: Divide by a two-digit number by trying its multiples, and then by taking away chunks you can work out, and find out why every choice of chunks ends on the same answer.
writeup.look: A ladder of multiples beside a long division frame on the left, and a bar with a column of chunk cards on the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Chunk Ladder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: on the first two phases the rungs written and the steps finished, and on the last two the running total of the chunk sizes taken, climbing as each chunk leaves the bar, with the dividend written beside it. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The working area is split into two panels by a near-black rule at 600. The left panel holds the working window across its top, 520 by 60 at 64,210, with the number being divided and its place name, a long division frame under it, 330 by 380 at 64,280, and the ladder of multiples climbing beside the frame, 170 by 440 at 414,280, nine rungs with the divisor times one at the foot. A rung is written in rose only as the climb reaches it, never printed in advance; the first rung bigger than the working number lights as too big, the climb stops there, and the rung under it is the one taken. The left slot sits under the frame, 200 by 50 at 64,670, and refuses a number as big as the divisor, springing it back with the rung that still fits lit and nothing marked, and the bring down arrow waits unlit until the slot holds a number. The right panel holds the bar for the dividend, 80 by 440 standing at 626,280, in deep blue, which shortens from the top as chunks leave it and keeps its full outline drawn so the part taken is still seen. Beside it stand the chunk cards, ten, twenty, fifty and a hundred times the divisor, each 150 by 60 from 726,280, with a typed chunk card under them, and each card shows both its chunk size and what it takes away. The chunk column, 150 by 440 at 896,280, writes each chunk size in green as it is taken with what it took away in rose beside it. When what is left is smaller than the divisor the bar refuses any more cards, the column is added under a rule, the sum is written as the quotient and what is left, in vermilion, as the remainder. On the last phase the right panel splits down the middle into two lanes, each with its own bar, cards and column for the same dividend. The missing number bay folds down over the lower left panel when it is opened, four slots for dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder, and builds whichever one is left empty from the other three. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a rung, a leftover or a chunk size is asked for, with a chunk key that opens the typed chunk card, so any multiple the child can work out can be taken. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion; a multiple of the divisor, tried on a ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose; and a zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because what is left over is told by the dish or the slot it sits in, a quotient digit by the row it sits in, and a multiple by the rung or the column that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour, and every rule, bracket, cell edge and guide line is near-black. Grey never means faint: a zero in the quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A rung that is too big is never hidden. It stays lit above the rung that was taken, because seeing the multiple that did not fit is how the one that did is known to be the largest.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last division the child worked, the ladder rung that was too big still lit, and both chunk columns standing side by side on one quotient.

phases.win: the rung that passes the number lights as too big and the rung below it gives the quotient digit
phases.does: climbs the ladder a rung at a time until one rung is bigger than the number
phases.goal: write multiples of the divisor until one passes the number, and take the one before it
phases.says: Climb one rung at a time. Which rung is too big?
phases.check: How many times does twenty-four go into one hundred? Write the rungs until one is too big.
phases.feels: the rung that is too big is not a mistake, it is the rung that proves the one below it is the largest that fits
phases.hands: Write ninety-one on the board with twenty-two beside it. Have the class build the twenty-two times table one line at a time, and after each line ask whether it is still under ninety-one. Stop the moment one line passes it. Ask which line gives the answer, and why the line that passed had to be written at all.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which rung did you stop on? Second rung, the phase's: have you written the rung above it? Third rung: the divisor is cut to eleven and the ladder climbs toward fifty, so every rung can be checked by eye. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: writing one more line feels like extra work, and a multiple that is somewhere close looks like the one being asked for.
wrong.move: stops at sixteen times three, forty-eight, because it looks near enough to seventy-five, and writes three.
wrong.screen: the leftover under the child's rung, twenty-seven, is offered to the left slot and springs back, because twenty-seven is bigger than sixteen. The climb then carries on from that rung: sixty-four fits, and eighty passes seventy-five and lights as too big. The child's three stays written beside the four the ladder settles on.

wrong.why: the climb ends on the passing rung, and the last number written is the one the hand is resting on.
wrong.move: takes the rung that is too big, because it is the last one written.
wrong.screen: the too-big rung is dragged toward the frame and will not land: eighty is laid against seventy-five as two bars side by side, and the longer runs past the end of the shorter. The child's five stays in the quotient cell, and the rung below it lights as the last one that fits, with nothing marked.

phases.screen: a two-digit divisor at the foot of an empty ladder, with the number to divide in the working window
phases.soWhat: Write multiples of the divisor until one passes the number, and take the one before it.
phases.concept: Try multiples until one is too big

phases.win: the leftover slides down beside the next digit and makes the number the next step divides
phases.does: works out what is left at that step and writes it before bringing the next digit down
phases.goal: what is left at each step joins the next digit to make the next number
phases.says: What is left here? Where will it go next?
phases.check: Divide four thousand and ninety-five by thirteen. Say what is left at every step, the middle one included.
phases.feels: the leftover is the piece of the next number that was already there before the digit came down
phases.hands: Work six thousand five hundred and seventy-four divided by eighteen on the board, the division this topic's worked example uses. At the middle step, once eighteen has gone into one hundred and seventeen tens six times, stop and ask what is left. Write the nine tens in coloured chalk before the four comes down, and ask where ninety-four came from.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which rung did this step take? Second rung, the phase's: what is the working number take away that rung? Third rung: the frame is cut to a two-step division, and the child fills the one slot between the steps. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the worked example states what is left at its first and last steps and skips the middle one, so skipping it looks like the way it is done.
wrong.move: skips the leftover at a middle step, then does not know where the next number came from.
wrong.screen: the bring down arrow stays unlit and the left slot at the middle step is lit empty, with the rung taken and the working number above it. The subtraction is run in the frame, one hundred and seventeen take away one hundred and eight, and the nine tens drop into the slot and slide down beside the four, so the ninety-four the next step divides is seen being made.

wrong.why: one fourteen fits, and a leftover looks like a leftover whatever its size.
wrong.move: takes fourteen once out of thirty-four tens and tries to carry twenty tens on.
wrong.screen: the left slot springs the twenty back, because twenty is bigger than the divisor, and lights the rung for two fourteens, twenty-eight, which still fits under thirty-four. The child's one stays written beside the quotient cell, and the step runs again with six tens dropping into the slot.

phases.screen: a division part way through, with the left slot empty at a middle step
phases.soWhat: What is left at each step joins the next digit to make the next number.
phases.concept: Say what is left at every step

phases.win: the bar shrinks below the divisor and the chunk column adds up to the quotient
phases.does: takes away chunks one after another, writing each chunk size, until too little is left to go round
phases.goal: chunks of the divisor that are easy to work out are taken away until less than the divisor is left
phases.says: Take away a chunk you can work out. How much is left now?
phases.check: Share eight hundred and forty among fifteen, taking fifty first and then a smaller chunk. What do your chunk sizes add up to?
phases.feels: any handful you can work out will do, and the handfuls you write down are the answer
phases.hands: Give each group three hundred beans, twelve cups, and two cards reading ten and five. They choose a card and put that many beans in every cup at once, writing the card's number each time. When too few beans are left to go round, they add up the numbers they wrote, and count the beans in one cup to see if it agrees.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which chunk did you take last? Second rung, the phase's: is what is left smaller than the divisor yet? Third rung: the bar is cut to a hundred and twenty for twelve, and the child takes a chunk of ten and adds the column. The number pad and the chunk key stay open.

wrong.why: the amounts taken away are the big numbers written down the working, and adding what is written down looks like the last step.
wrong.move: adds up the amounts taken away, six hundred, three hundred and sixty and forty-eight, instead of the chunk sizes.
wrong.screen: the child's sum is written under the column, one thousand and eight, and it matches the dividend exactly: the amounts taken away rebuild all the eggs, not one shop's share. The chunk sizes are then lit one at a time, fifty, thirty and four, and added under their own rule to eighty-four. Both sums stay drawn, with what each one counts written beside it.

wrong.why: the round chunks are the ones that feel like chunks, and a small one like four does not look worth taking.
wrong.move: stops after the fifty and the thirty and writes eighty, with forty-eight eggs still left for twelve shops.
wrong.screen: the bar refuses to close while forty-eight stands on it, because forty-eight is bigger than twelve, and every shop's cup lights as able to take more. The typed chunk card opens beside the bar, and the child's eighty stays in the column's total line until the last chunk is taken.

phases.screen: a bar for the dividend with the chunk cards beside it and an empty chunk column
phases.soWhat: Chunks of the divisor that are easy to work out are taken away until less than the divisor is left, and the chunk sizes add up to the quotient.

phases.win: the two chunk columns end on one number and the two quotients stand level
phases.does: takes the second bar apart with different chunks and adds its column
phases.goal: different chunks add up to the same quotient
phases.says: Use different chunks this time. Does the answer change?
phases.check: One friend shares six hundred and twenty-four among twenty-four using chunks of twenty and six. Another uses ten, ten and six. Do they agree?
phases.feels: the lists of chunks disagree and the share in every part does not, because the share was never in any one chunk
phases.hands: Let two groups share the same number of beans into the same number of cups, but give them different cards. When both are done, compare the beans in one cup, and then compare the lists of numbers each group wrote down. Ask why the lists differ and the cups do not.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the first lane's column add up to? Second rung, the phase's: what does yours add up to? Third rung: both lanes are cut to forty-eight shared by four, and the child runs chunks of ten and two in one lane and six and six in the other. The number pad and the chunk key stay open.

wrong.why: two lists of different numbers look like two different sums, and the worked example uses one set as if it were the method.
wrong.move: thinks a different set of chunks must give a different answer, or that only the set in the worked example is allowed.
wrong.screen: the second lane runs the child's own chunks beside the first lane's, the two columns plainly different, and both are added on the same tick and land on eighty-four. One shop's eggs from each lane are then drawn side by side, the same count, with both columns left standing.

wrong.why: twenty was a comfortable chunk in the other lane, and it is carried across without looking at what this bar has left.
wrong.move: takes twenty more for each shop after the seventy, two hundred and forty, when only one hundred and sixty-eight are left.
wrong.screen: the card is dragged to the bar and will not land: two hundred and forty is laid against the hundred and sixty-eight still standing, and runs past its end. The card goes back to the stack, the child's twenty stays written at the foot of the column with nothing marked, and ten for each shop is offered beside it, a hundred and twenty, which fits.

phases.screen: the same dividend loaded into both lanes, with the first lane already finished
phases.soWhat: Different chunks add up to the same quotient.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment the second lane's column is added. The two columns stand side by side with different chunk sizes in them, and their sums are written under their rules on the same tick. They land on one number, and the two quotients slide together into a single line across the panel while both emptied bars light at once, each holding the same small leftover. A third set of chunks can be run as often as a finger likes, and it lands on the same number every time. Nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the ladder in the left panel is empty with the divisor written at its foot and the number to divide in the working window, while the bar in the right panel stands full with the chunk cards stacked beside it and unused. On the second a division stands part way through, its first leftover written, the left slot empty at the middle step and the bring down arrow unlit. On the third the bar for the dividend stands full length with the chunk cards beside it and the chunk column empty. On the fourth both lanes hold the same dividend, the first finished with its column added and the second still full. The running count at the top left holds the rungs written or the chunks taken, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the foot of the ladder, or the empty left slot, or the top chunk card, or the second bar, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many times the divisor fits. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any dividend up to five digits and any divisor up to ninety-nine, with the ladder, both chunk lanes and the missing number bay open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on trying multiples of a two-digit divisor, saying what is left at every step, taking away chunks, and showing that different chunks give the same quotient.
voiceLines: A two-digit divisor and a ladder beside it. Climb until one rung is too big.
Climb one rung at a time. Which rung is too big?
What is left here? Where will it go next?
Take away a chunk you can work out. How much is left now?
Use different chunks this time. Does the answer change?
A new division. Write the first rung before anything is tried.
Free play. Any dividend, any divisor up to ninety-nine, with both lanes and the missing number bay open.
Go back to the last rung that fitted, and say what is left under it.
Every step said out loud, and every set of chunks landing on the same quotient.

observations.why: A two-digit divisor's times table is not known by heart, so its multiples are written until one is too big.
observations.soWhat: Trying multiples until one is too big finds each quotient digit, and it is trial and check, nothing more.
observations.observe: The climb stopped at the first rung that passed the number, and the rung under it gave the digit.

observations.why: What is left joins the next digit, and the next number to divide is made from the two of them.
observations.soWhat: Say what is left at every step, the middle ones included, where the worked example skips its nine tens.
observations.observe: The left slot had to be filled before the next digit could come down.

observations.why: Each chunk size is how many each part got that time, and each amount taken is that many for every part at once.
observations.soWhat: The quotient is the sum of the chunk sizes, not the sum of what was taken away.
observations.observe: The chunk column added up to the quotient, and the amounts taken away added up to the dividend.

observations.why: Each set of chunks shares the same total into the same number of parts, only in different handfuls.
observations.soWhat: Any chunks will do, as long as they are taken away until less than the divisor is left.
observations.observe: Two lanes with different chunks ended on the same quotient.

source_tool.description: The stage holds two working areas side by side. On the left a ladder of multiples climbs beside a long division frame: the divisor times one, times two, times three and upwards, each rung written as it is reached, and the climb stops at the first rung that passes the number being divided, which is lit as too big so that the rung below it is the one taken. A left slot at every step must be filled before the next digit comes down, and it will not take a number as big as the divisor. On the right a bar stands for the dividend beside a column of chunk cards, ten, twenty, fifty and a hundred times the divisor, and a card that takes any chunk the child types. Each chunk taken away is drawn leaving the bar, its size written in a running column, until what remains is smaller than the divisor. The column of chunk sizes is then added, and that sum is the quotient. A second lane can run the same dividend with different chunks, and the two quotients stand together at the end. A missing number bay takes any three of dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder and builds the fourth from the rule that ties them.
source_tool.art_direction: A ladder of multiples beside a bar / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a tray of counters and a row of plates, digit cards under place headings, sticks tied in bundles, a long division frame with its bracket, a ladder of multiples, a strip of cells, a story card, and two rails tied at every stop.

Equal shares are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a plate or a part is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are on it, and anything counted one at a time is drawn in rows of ten so that no more than twenty loose things ever have to be counted singly.

What is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the shares, in a dish or a slot of its own, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never tucked under a share and never left to be guessed from a gap.
A division is always written with every place headed. The number being divided at a step is shown with its place name, so fifteen tens is never drawn as a bare fifteen.

Every zero in a quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as the other digits and is never dimmed, shrunk or dropped. A zero is written only where the number being divided is smaller than the divisor, and a leading zero may stand or be left off, but a zero after the first digit always stands.
What is left at every step is drawn in its own slot before the next digit comes down, and it slides down to join that digit so the next number can be seen being made.
A remainder is written as a number. A zero standing in front of its other digits is lifted off and set aside, never written into the answer.
No stage ever shows a number for a division by zero. Where one is asked, the stage says it is not possible and draws nothing to share into.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a counter, a digit or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; and what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion. Those four hold from the plates to the frame to the story card in every tool of this chapter. A multiple of the divisor, whether it is being tried on the ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose, so the chunks can be added up without being mistaken for the share. A zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey, and grey never means faint: it is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, because it is holding a place. All of that holds in greyscale, because what is left over is told apart by the dish or the left slot it sits in, and a quotient digit by the row it sits in, before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

phase_map.concept: Try multiples until one is too big
Say what is left at every step

placement.where: After beans have been packed into cups a chunk at a time by hand, with different groups choosing different chunks. The tool is what keeps two sets of chunks for one dividend on the stage at the same time, so the two quotients are seen to agree rather than being compared from memory.

answer_key.rule: To divide by a two-digit number, write its multiples, times one, times two and on, until one is bigger than the number being divided; the one before it gives the quotient digit. Say what is left at every step, because what is left joins the next digit to make the next number to divide. In the partial quotient method, take away any multiples of the divisor you can work out, such as ten or fifty times it, until what is left is zero or smaller than the divisor. The chunk sizes add up to the quotient and what is left is the remainder. Different chunks give the same quotient. A missing dividend is divisor times quotient, add the remainder, and a missing divisor is the dividend take away the remainder, divided by the quotient.
answer_key.wrong: The ladder is climbed again from times one with each rung said aloud, what is left is written in at the step that skipped it, and the chunk column is added once more. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: 16 times 1 is 16, times 2 is 32, times 3 is 48 and times 4 is 64.
16 times 5 is 80, which is more than 75, so 5 is too many.
So 16 goes into 75 four times, and 75 take away 64 leaves 11.
items.answer: 4 times, with 11 left, because 16 times 5 is 80, which is more than 75
items.question: How many times does 16 go into 75? Write multiples of 16 until one is too big.
items.checkpoint: Write multiples of the divisor until one passes the number; the one before it gives the quotient digit.
items.misconception: Stopping at the first multiple that looks close, without checking that the next one really is too big.

steps: 59 hundreds divided by 14 is 4 hundreds, because 14 times 4 is 56, and 3 hundreds are left.
The 3 hundreds and 4 tens make 34 tens: 14 times 2 is 28, so 2 tens, with 6 tens left.
The 6 tens and 8 ones make 68 ones: 14 times 4 is 56, so 4 ones, with 12 left, and 12 is smaller than 14.
items.question: Divide 5948 by 14, saying what is left at every step.
items.checkpoint: Say what is left at every step, because it joins the next digit to make the next number to divide.
items.misconception: Skipping the leftover at a middle step, then not knowing where the next number came from.

steps: 50 for each of 12 shops uses 600 eggs, and 1008 take away 600 leaves 408.
30 more for each shop uses 360, and 408 take away 360 leaves 48.
48 is 12 times 4, so 4 more each leaves nothing: 50, 30 and 4 make 84 for each shop.
items.answer: 84 eggs for each shop, because 50, 30 and 4 add up to 84
items.question: 1008 eggs are shared equally among 12 shops. Take away chunks: 50 for each shop first, then 30 each, then whatever is left.
items.checkpoint: Take away chunks of the divisor that you can work out, until less than the divisor is left; the chunk sizes add up to the quotient.
items.misconception: Adding up the amounts taken away, 600, 360 and 48, instead of the chunk sizes 50, 30 and 4.

steps: 70 for each shop uses 840, and 1008 take away 840 leaves 168.
10 more each uses 120, leaving 48, and 4 more each uses the last 48.
70, 10 and 4 add up to 84, the same quotient as 50, 30 and 4.
items.answer: Yes, still 84 each, because 70, 10 and 4 also add up to 84
items.question: Share the same 1008 eggs among 12 shops using the chunks 70, 10 and 4. Is each share still the same?
items.checkpoint: Different chunks give the same quotient, as long as they are taken away until less than the divisor is left.
items.misconception: Thinking a different set of chunks must give a different answer, or that only one set is allowed.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many times does 17 go into 90, and what is left?
items.final_answer: 5 times, with 5 left, because 17 times 5 is 85 and 17 times 6 is 102

items.question: Write the multiples of 19 up to 19 times 5. How many times does 19 go into 83?
items.final_answer: 19, 38, 57, 76 and 95, so 19 goes into 83 four times, with 7 left

items.question: 150 tens divided by 21 gives 7 tens. How many tens are left?
Divide 3875 by 17, and say what is left at every step.
items.final_answer: 227 remainder 16: 4 hundreds are left after the first step, 13 tens after the second, and 16 at the end

items.question: A school sends 1350 books equally to 18 libraries. Use chunks of 50, 20 and 5 to find how many each library gets.
items.final_answer: 75 books each, because 50, 20 and 5 add up to 75 and nothing is left

items.question: Find 2691 divided by 23 by taking away chunks. What is the quotient?
items.final_answer: 117, for example as 100, 10 and 7 twenty-threes, with nothing left

items.question: Two children divide 1904 by 28. One uses the chunks 50, 10 and 8, and the other uses 60 and 8. Show that both get the same quotient.
items.final_answer: Both get 68: 50, 10 and 8 make 68, and 60 and 8 make 68, with nothing left either way

items.question: The divisor is 26, the quotient is 58 and the remainder is 9. What is the dividend?
items.final_answer: 1517, because 26 times 58 is 1508 and 1508 add 9 is 1517; dividing 1517 by 26 gives 58 remainder 9 again

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: writes the divisor times one, times two and upwards, and lights the first rung that is too big
takes what is left at every step and refuses a number as big as the divisor
brings the next digit down beside what is left once the slot is filled
take away ten, twenty, fifty or a hundred times the divisor, or a typed chunk
writes each chunk size taken away and adds them up at the end
runs the same dividend with different chunks beside the first
builds the missing one of dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder from the other three

teaching_notes: Pack beans into cups before the tool is opened, a chunk at a time, and let different groups choose different chunks. Every group ends with the same number in each cup, and that surprise is the lesson of the second half of this topic. For the first half, the divisor's times table is not known by heart, so write its multiples on the board, times one, times two and upwards, and stop at the first one that is too big. The worked example for this topic does exactly that, and it states what is left at its first step and at its last, but not at the middle one. Eighteen goes into one hundred and seventeen six times, and nine tens are left. Those nine tens and the four ones make the ninety-four ones divided next, and a child who never hears the nine tens does not know where ninety-four came from. Make stating the leftover a habit at every step; the tool will not bring a digit down until it has been written. The chapter's self-assessment asks a child to estimate a quotient, which the chapter never teaches. Trying multiples until one is too big is trial and check, and it is taught here as that, not as estimating, which is taught nowhere in these pages. The two Critical Thinking questions for this topic have divisors of three hundred and of a hundred, bigger than any divisor the chapter teaches; the missing number bay will build them, but say so. The closing skills page seats a cricket ground in six blocks, three divisions to a block, all of them exact. Eleven of its eighteen divisions are by ten or by a number with two digits, so it belongs here, and the other seven are by one digit, which the long division topic already covers. The page never says that a block's people are the sum of its three quotients, though that is the only reading that answers it; say so before the class starts adding, and the six blocks then hold six thousand seven hundred and sixty-nine people. The lab that closes the chapter uses digit cards, with a card drawn from a pack as the divisor and a jack counting as eleven.
generation_prompt: Build a two-digit division tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, its working area split into two panels. The left panel holds a long division frame with a ladder of multiples climbing beside it: rungs for the divisor times one, times two and upwards are written one at a time as they are reached, the climb stops at the first rung bigger than the number in the working window, that rung is lit as too big, and the rung below it gives the quotient digit. A left slot at every step must be filled before the bring down arrow lights, and it refuses a number as big as the divisor, with nothing marked. The right panel holds a bar standing for the dividend, which shortens as chunks leave it, beside chunk cards for ten, twenty, fifty and a hundred times the divisor and a card that takes a typed chunk. Each chunk taken away is drawn leaving the bar and its size is written in a running chunk column, until what remains is smaller than the divisor; the column is then added and the sum written as the quotient, with what remains as the remainder. A second lane under the first runs the same dividend with different chunks, and both quotients stand together at the end. A missing number bay takes any three of dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder and builds the fourth, dividing the dividend less the remainder by the quotient for a missing divisor. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Write the divisor's multiples until one is too big. Take the one before it. Say what is left every time. Or take away chunks you can work out. Add the chunks to get the quotient.
